extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (restriction practice training); patent prosecution practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on when and how to require restriction among genus, species, linking, and Markush claims during patent examination, including definitions, tests for distinctness, showing serious burden, election procedures, and examination consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two statutory criteria for a restriction requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Every restriction requirement has two criteria: the inventions, as claimed, must be independent or distinct; and there would be a serious burden on the examiner if restriction were not required. (MPEP 803, subsection I)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both criteria must be satisfied to support a restriction requirement. Cite MPEP 803.

rubrics_metrics.name: Serious burden requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A serious burden exists when the search and examination for one of the claimed inventions is not required for another of the claimed inventions. (MPEP 808.02)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the search/exam effort needed for one invention does not sufficiently overlap with that for another, a serious burden may be present. The examiner must explain why such burden exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Showing serious burden — reasons and prima facie showing
rubrics_metrics.description: The examiner must provide reasons why a serious burden would exist to support a restriction requirement. A serious burden may be prima facie shown if the inventions have separate classification or separate status in the art when the inventions are classifiable together or a different field of search as defined in MPEP 808.02. The prima facie showing may be rebutted by the applicant. (MPEP 803)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document classification differences or art-search differences to make a prima facie case; be prepared for applicant rebuttal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Showing serious burden — different field of search examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Serious burden may be established based on a different field of search if it is necessary to search for one of the inventions in a manner not likely to result in finding art pertinent to the other invention(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include searching different classes/subclasses, searching different electronic resources, or employing different search queries. Even when inventions are classified together, explain how the searches differ. (FP 8.21.03)

rubrics_metrics.name: Obvious variants are not distinct inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinctness between related inventions requires that at least one invention would not have been obvious over the other (i.e., that the inventions are not obvious variants). If the claims on their face are obvious over each other, restriction is not proper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: method of connecting two parts — one embodiment uses a screw, another a nail; these are obvious variants and should be grouped. See MPEP 806.04(h).

rubrics_metrics.name: Restriction not proper when no serious burden exists
rubrics_metrics.description: If the search and examination of all the claims in an application can be made without serious burden, the examiner must examine all of the claims on the merits, even if the claims are drawn to independent or distinct inventions. (MPEP 803)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not require restriction merely because inventions are distinct if combined examination is feasible without serious burden.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restriction not proper when express admission of obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: If there is an express admission that the claimed inventions are obvious over each other within the meaning of 35 U.S.C. 103, restriction should not be required. (MPEP section 803)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for statements in the specification or prosecution history that concede obviousness among the claimed inventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restriction not proper when claims are not distinct (overlap genus/subgenus/species)
rubrics_metrics.description: When the inventions are not distinct as claimed, restriction is never proper. Example: Claim 1. A transgenic animal comprising SEQ ID No 1. Claim 2. A transgenic rodent comprising SEQ ID No 1. Claim 3. A transgenic mouse comprising SEQ ID No 1. Restriction among claims 1, 2 and 3 is not proper because claims 1, 2 and 3 overlap in scope as genus, subgenus and species claim. (MPEP 806)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not restrict claims that overlap in scope as genus/subgenus/species.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restriction not proper when claims define same essential characteristics of a single disclosed embodiment
rubrics_metrics.description: When the claims define the same essential characteristics of a single disclosed embodiment of an invention, restriction is not proper. (MPEP 806.03)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Claim 1. A compound of formula 1. Claim 2. A compound having the x-ray diffraction pattern as depicted in Fig 12. Both claims define the same essential characteristics of a single disclosed embodiment and should not be restricted from each other.

rubrics_metrics.name: What are species
rubrics_metrics.description: Species are always specifically different embodiments of an invention. Species typically are disclosed as examples or figures in the specification. Species may be independent or related. (MPEP 806.04(e))
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify species in the disclosure (examples, figures) and evaluate distinctness per other tests.

rubrics_metrics.name: What is a genus claim
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim that encompasses two or more disclosed embodiments (species) within its scope is considered to be a generic or genus claim. (MPEP 806.04(d) and 806.04(e))
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize genus claims whether written as a generic claim, a Markush, or as a series of single species claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three ways to claim a genus
rubrics_metrics.description: Three ways to claim a genus: (1) as a series of single species claims (e.g., Claim 1: An orange. Claim 2: A lemon); (2) as a Markush claim reading upon plural species (e.g., a citrus fruit selected from the group consisting of an orange or a lemon); (3) encompassed by a linking claim which reads upon but is not necessarily limited to plural species disclosed in the specification (e.g., Claim 4: A citrus fruit).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify which form the genus takes—series, Markush, or linking—because examination/restriction practice differs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test for distinctness between species
rubrics_metrics.description: Species are distinct when: (1) each species, as claimed, requires a mutually exclusive characteristic not required for the other species; AND (2) the species, as claimed, are not obvious variants of each other. (MPEP 806.04(f))
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply both prongs: mutually exclusive characteristic and non-obviousness between species to find distinctness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Election of species — form paragraphs and provisional election
rubrics_metrics.description: When an election of species is appropriate, FP 8.01 or 8.02 should be used to communicate the requirement. Use FP 8.01 when claims limited to species are present; use FP 8.02 when no claims limited to species are present. A restriction requirement may contain a requirement to elect a single invention and/or a provisional requirement to elect a species for examination purposes. (FP 8.01 / 8.02)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select the appropriate form paragraph depending on whether species-limited claims exist; explain why species are independent or distinct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Linking claim — definition and typical kinds
rubrics_metrics.description: A linking claim is a claim which, if allowable, would prevent restriction between two or more otherwise properly divisible (restrictable) inventions. Linking claims and linked inventions are usually either product claims linking properly divisible product inventions, or process claims linking properly divisible process inventions. Most kinds of linking claims are genus claims linking species claims or subcombination claims linking plural combinations that require the subcombination. (MPEP 809 and 809.03)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize linking claims because an allowable linking claim prevents restriction and must be examined with the elected invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of linking claims on restriction and examination
rubrics_metrics.description: If a linking claim links distinct inventions, restriction can be required when there are linking claims and claims to distinct inventions. If a linked invention is elected, the linking claims are examined with the elected invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: genus linking claim (Claim 1) links species claims (Claims 2–4); Claim 1 cannot be restricted from claims 2–4 and must be examined with the elected species.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subcombination linking — example and effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Subcombination linking occurs where combination claims are linked by a subcombination claim. Example: combination kits (Claims 1–2) and a primer-only claim (Claim 3) where Claim 3 is a linking claim and will be examined with the elected combination. (MPEP 806.05(c)(subsection III))
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not restrict a linking subcombination from the combination if it links them; examine linking claim with elected combination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allowable linking claims — consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: When a linking claim is allowable, a restriction requirement between the inventions it links cannot be maintained. The restriction requirement should be withdrawn, even if claims to non-elected linked inventions have been canceled. Any claim(s) depending from or otherwise requiring all the limitations of the allowable linking claim(s) will be rejoined and fully examined for patentability. The Office must provide Applicant with an opportunity to reinstate canceled claims when a restriction requirement is withdrawn based on the allowability of the linking claim. (MPEP 809.03 and 821.04(a))
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If linking claim becomes allowable, withdraw restriction, rejoin dependent claims, and offer opportunity to reinstate canceled claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical tips on linking claims (form paragraph and grouping practice)
rubrics_metrics.description: When requiring a restriction involving linking claims per MPEP 809.03, the linking claims should not appear in the list of claims for any particular group. The linking claims appear only in FP 8.12. When requiring a restriction involving genus-species linking claims per MPEP 809.02, there are no groupings and the linking claims appear as the generic claims in FP 8.01.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place linking claims correctly in restriction paperwork (FP 8.12 or FP 8.01) to reflect linking status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Markush claim — definition/overview
rubrics_metrics.description: A Markush claim recites a plurality of alternatively usable substances or members. Alternatives may be 'selected from the group consisting of A, B and C.' The group of alternatives A, B, and C is commonly referred to as a 'Markush group.' (MPEP 803.02)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify Markush groups and members when assessing possible restriction issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: When a Markush claim may be restricted
rubrics_metrics.description: A Markush claim may include independent and distinct inventions and be subject to restriction. Restriction is proper where two or more members of the group are so unrelated and diverse that a prior art reference would anticipate the claim with respect to one of the members but would not render the claim obvious with respect to the other members. If restriction is proper, then a provisional election of a single species may be required. (MPEP 803.02)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess relatedness/diversity of Markush members and whether prior art affects members differently to justify restriction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Markush practical tip — few or closely related members
rubrics_metrics.description: If the members of the Markush group are sufficiently few in number or so closely related that a search and examination of the entire claim can be made without serious burden, the examiner must examine all the members of the Markush group in the claim on the merits, even though they may be directed to independent and distinct inventions. (MPEP 803.02)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not require restriction of a Markush claim when full examination of all members is feasible without serious burden.

rubrics_metrics.name: Markush examination sequence when species elected or found unallowable
rubrics_metrics.description: Should the elected species be found allowable, the search/examination of the Markush type claim will be extended to determine the patentability of the claim, including the non-elected species. Should the elected species be found not allowable, the provisional election will be given effect and examination limited to the elected species. If examiner finds art on another species, the examiner does NOT extend search to cover ALL the non-elected species. (MPEP 803.02)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand when to extend examination to other members (if elected species allowable) versus when provisional election limits examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Markush election canceled species consequence
rubrics_metrics.description: Should the examiner require election of a species recited in a Markush claim, and the elected species is canceled in response to a prior art rejection, such response is considered proper and the examination of the Markush type claim will be extended to the non-elected species to determine the patentability of the claim. The next Office action could be made final if appropriate. (MPEP 803.02 and 821.03)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If elected species is canceled due to prior art, extend to non-elected species and consider finality rules for the next action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examination practice contrasts: Markush vs Linking claims (rules and examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Detailed practice differences between Markush (MPEP 803.02) and Linking claims (MPEP 809) illustrated by examples: e.g., (1) If the species of claim 2 is elected, claim 3 would be withdrawn from consideration; (2) If prior art is found against claim 2, both claims 1 and 2 would be rejected; (3A) For Markush: If claim 2 is allowable, allow claim 2 and extend the search and examination for the species of claim 3; (3B) For Markush: Search/examination is limited to species of the Markush group of claim 1; (4) For Markush: If prior art is found against claim 3, bring claim 3 back into consideration and reject both claims 1 and 3; For Linking: (3) If claim 2 is allowable, allow claim 2 and examiner may extend search and examination for any species encompassed by claim 1; (4A) If prior art is found (a species other than elected), reject claim 1 and examiner is not required to extend search to claim 3; (4B) If prior art found is the species lime, bring claim 3 back into consideration and reject both claims 1 and 3; (5) For both sets: If claim 1 is allowable, then allow claims 1, 2 and 3.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the specific Markush vs linking rules for withdrawing/withholding claims, extending searches, and effect of prior art; treat linking claims more broadly in allowing extension to other species when appropriate, but do not extend in some linking prior-art scenarios.
